messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane is a 48-year-old Māori man who works as a roofer, married for over two decades, and until recently considered himself someone who had long since made peace with the harder parts of his life. He presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 47, describing a clinical picture that had been quietly consolidating for years before finally becoming impossible to manage.

The assault occurred several years ago. Tane had been at a work function — a late evening gathering at a colleague's home — and had drunk more than usual. He remembers the smell of alcohol on the man who cornered him in a back room, the sound of a motorcycle idling outside that seemed to stretch time into something unbearable, and the particular helplessness of a body that would not do what he told it to. He did not tell anyone. He drove home, showered, and returned to work the following Monday. He had convinced himself, with the kind of discipline that had served him well on rooftops and in hard weather, that it was something he could simply not think about.

What he did not anticipate was the way the world kept finding him. A news segment about sexual violence — the kind that appears without warning between weather and sport — would stop him cold in his living room, and within seconds he would be somewhere else entirely, the memory arriving not as recollection but as presence, vivid and immediate in a way that ordinary memories simply were not. He described it as the event being more real than anything that had actually happened that day. Sometimes there was no image at all, only a wave of emotion — grief, shame, something that felt like drowning — arriving without context or warning. And when he did remember clearly, what followed was an overwhelming grief that he could neither explain to his wife nor outrun. These memory intrusions, in turn, sharpened his vigilance to the very cues that had preceded them: the smell of alcohol at a family barbecue, the sound of a motorcycle passing on the street outside a job site, a headline glimpsed on a phone screen. Each trigger fed the memory, and each memory primed him to find the next trigger faster.

In response to this, Tane built a life structured around prevention. He began refusing jobs that required prolonged physical exertion in heat — the kind of full-body exhaustion that reminded him of that night, of a body beyond his control — telling his crew he had a back problem. He started monitoring his food intake with a precision that surprised even him, eating by strict rule, finding in that control something the rest of his life no longer offered. And he worked. He scheduled himself into every available hour, took on extra contracts, stayed on rooftops until the light failed, because busyness was the only reliable way to keep the memories from surfacing. But these strategies, over time, began to work against him in ways he had not foreseen. The rigid avoidance of physical stress meant he never processed the somatic dimension of what had happened; the controlled eating, though it gave momentary relief, left him feeling brittle and oddly exposed when routines were disrupted; and the relentless busyness, while suppressing intrusions during the day, seemed to make the evenings — when the work stopped and the house went quiet — into ambushes. His strategies had become their own triggers, the moments when control slipped revealing the very memories the control was meant to contain.

His marriage had become quieter in ways neither he nor his wife had named directly. She had noticed his distance, his refusal of certain social events where alcohol was present, the way he sometimes left the room when the television news ran certain stories. He had told her nothing. What finally brought him to seek help was his eldest son's twenty-first birthday party, where the smell of beer and the sound of motorcycles arriving in the driveway converged at once, and Tane found himself sitting in his car for forty minutes unable to go back inside. He wants, more than anything, to stop being ambushed by his own life. What he fears most is that there is no version of himself that gets to come home intact.
